title: Pyrrhus and the Costly Victory
text:
In 280 BC King Pyrrhus of Epirus, one of the finest generals of his age, crossed to Italy to help the Greek city of Tarentum against Rome. He brought a professional army trained in the Macedonian style, together with war elephants, which the Romans had never faced. He beat the Romans at Heraclea, but at heavy cost.

In 279 BC the two sides met again near Asculum in Apulia. Plutarch says that the fighting went on over two days. On the first day the wooded, broken ground hampered Pyrrhus's cavalry and elephants. On the second he seized level ground, and his phalanx and elephants finally drove the Romans back to their camp. Plutarch cites figures of six thousand Roman dead, while Pyrrhus's own records admitted about 3,500 of his men.

The numbers favored Pyrrhus, but the arithmetic did not. Plutarch reports that when someone congratulated him on the victory, Pyrrhus replied that one more such victory would utterly undo him. He had lost a large part of the army he had brought from Greece, along with most of his friends and chief commanders, and he could not replace them. Rome, by contrast, refilled its legions quickly from its large manpower, as if from a fountain, and its anger only grew.

Pyrrhus soon left for Sicily, and in 275 BC he returned to Greece. His name became a word for a victory that costs more than it gains.
lesson: Count the cost of winning, not only the result. A victory that drains resources you cannot replace may set you up to lose the larger contest.
